admicom-x-wunderdog-evals-cloud-agents:
Opening slide. Say who you are and what the next hour is about: how to know an AI agent actually does its job (evals), and how to let agents work on their own in the cloud (cloud agents). Tomorrow's workshop builds on this, so everything today is something we will use.

anatomy-of-a-cloud-session:
What happens in a cloud session. Something starts it: a person, a schedule, an API call or a GitHub event. It gets its own isolated VM. With --cloud it clones your GitHub repo at your current branch (routines start from the default branch). The setup script installs dependencies, the agent edits and runs code, checks run, and the result becomes a pull request. Routines push to branches starting with claude/. Other tools follow the same pattern: OpenAI Codex Cloud, GitHub Copilot cloud agent (earlier called coding agent) and Cursor Cloud Agents.

Key points
• One isolated VM per session
• Repo cloned from GitHub, not your local files
• Ends in a PR you review
• Same pattern across Codex, Copilot and Cursor

anatomy-of-a-plugin-eval:
This is how Claude Code's plugin evals look on disk. Each case is a folder under evals/ with a prompt.md and a graders folder. The prompt.md frontmatter sets limits like max_turns and allowed_tools. allowed_tools only grants read-only tools (Read, Glob, Grep, Skill and similar); writing files needs --allow-tools Write when you run it, as on the next slide. Each run starts in an empty folder, so input files like comments.json are added with case.yaml (add_dirs or a scaffold script). Here we use two graders: a regex on findings.json checks the result, and tool_used checks that the review-catalogue skill was actually called.

Key points
• One folder per case: prompt.md + graders/
• max_turns default is 10, max 200
• allowed_tools grants read-only tools; others need --allow-tools
• One grader checks the result, one checks the path the agent took

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals
anatomy-of-an-eval:
The words we will use for the rest of the talk, taken from Anthropic's eval post. A task is one test with an input and success criteria. A trial is one attempt at that task; you run several. The transcript is the full record of a trial: outputs, tool calls, reasoning. The outcome is the real end state, for example whether the file or database row actually exists. Graders each check one thing, and the score is the pass rate across trials.

Key points
• Task: input + what counts as success
• Trial: one attempt, run several
• Transcript: everything the agent did
• Outcome: the actual end state, not what the agent said
• Grader: checks one thing; score = pass rate (67% = 2 of 3)

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

capability-vs-regression:
Two kinds of eval suites. Capability evals ask what the agent can do well and should start with a low pass rate, so there is room to improve. Regression evals check that things that already work keep working, and should pass close to 100%. When a capability case passes reliably, it moves into the regression suite (Anthropic calls this graduating). The 18% and 98% numbers here are example values.

Key points
• Capability: hard cases, low score is expected
• Regression: should be near 100%
• A case moves to regression once it passes reliably
• rule-not-followed is an example case from our workshop skill

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
contributors-not-committers:
Cloud agents open PRs like any contributor; they do not merge. Here a hook PR breaks one eval case, a human reviewer asks for a change, and Claude pushes a fix. That is the Auto-fix pull requests feature: Claude watches the PR's GitHub events and pushes clear fixes for CI failures and review comments, and asks first when a comment is unclear. It needs the Claude GitHub App, is turned on per PR and does not handle merge conflicts. A human still approves and merges. The PR content is example data.

Key points
• Agent opens the PR, a human merges
• Auto-fix reacts to CI failures and review comments
• Needs the Claude GitHub App, per-PR toggle
• Keep branch protection on

credentials-stay-outside:
GitHub tokens never go inside the cloud VM. The agent runs git push as normal, and a GitHub proxy outside the VM adds the credentials. The proxy blocks branch deletes and pushes that are not branches, like tags. It does not limit which branches can be updated, so your GitHub branch protection rules are what protect main.

Key points
• Tokens stay outside the VM
• Proxy blocks tag pushes and branch deletes
• Branch protection on GitHub still matters

You can start several cloud sessions at once and each gets its own VM. Here three unrelated jobs run in parallel and each ends as its own PR. They all count against the same account rate limits, so more parallel sessions use your limits faster. There is no separate compute bill. The PR numbers are example data.

from-pair-programmer-to-teammate:
How the way we use AI for coding has changed, step by step. Autocomplete suggests the next line. Chat answers questions. A local agent edits and runs code while you watch. A cloud agent works while you are away and you review the result. Routines start on their own from a schedule or an event. Each step gives the agent more freedom and moves you from typing to reviewing.

Key points
• Your role moves from typing to reviewing
• Cloud agents work without you present
• Routines start themselves from triggers

from-skill-to-night-shift-to-routine:
Both flows grow the same way. Step 1: a skill you run by hand (/catalogue-reviews before a retro, /triage-ci when a build fails). Step 2: a scheduled task on your machine that runs it at set times. Step 3: a routine in the cloud that runs without your machine, on a schedule (at most hourly) or from an API call. Evals must pass before each step up, because each step means less human checking.

Key points
• Skill → scheduled task → routine
• Each step needs less of you
• Evals must pass before moving up

https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines
grade-the-outcome-not-the-claim:
The agent says the flaky test is fixed. Running the test 10 times shows 3 failures. Agents report success confidently even when it is not true, so graders should check the real result in the repo, not the agent's message. Anthropic's post uses a flight booking example: the agent says 'booked', but the check is whether the booking exists in the database.

Key points
• Agents can say 'done' when it isn't
• Check the end state: tests, files, data
• Flaky tests need repeated runs to catch
• The test output here is example data

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
line-1-review-comment-cataloguer:
Our main workshop flow. A skill reads the 'changes requested' comments from last week's merged PRs, groups them by problem type and counts them, then maps each problem type to an existing rule, skill or hook (or notes that none exists). It scores each suggested improvement from 100 to 0 by how many review comments it would prevent, highest first. A change only lands if the evals improve. Later a weekly routine runs it and posts a summary for the retro plus a draft PR. This is our design for the workshop, not an existing product; the counts on screen are example data.

Key points
• Input: review comments from merged PRs
• Output: problem types mapped to rules, skills, hooks
• Scored 100–0 by impact
• Eval gate stops bad suggestions
• Weekly routine feeds the retro
line-2-ci-health:
The second workshop flow. When main goes red, a triage-ci skill reads the logs and sorts the failure into flaky, broken or infrastructure. Flaky tests go into a ledger that tracks repeat offenders across runs. A scheduled task checks main every morning; a routine with an API trigger can start the same work in the cloud when CI fails. The result is a draft fix PR that a human reviews. Claude Code's auto-fix already handles CI on a single PR; this flow watches main over time. triage-ci is our workshop skill, not a built-in one.

Key points
• Diagnose before rerunning
• Ledger tracks flaky tests over time
• Morning scheduled task, cloud routine on CI failure
• Ends in a draft PR for a human

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web

meet-the-tire-plant:
The six stations are the six steps of an agentic development flow. Order terminal = ticket. Spec station = planning agent. Tire builder = coding agent. Curing press and X-ray = CI. Final inspection = code review. Shipping dock = release. The overhead chain is the harness, Claude Code, which moves every task through every step and gives it context, tools and permissions. The robot arm is the model. You can switch the model and the harness stays the same.

Key points
• Ticket → planning → coding → CI → review → release
• Chain = harness (Claude Code)
• Robot arm = model, it can be swapped
more-lines-for-the-same-plant:
The same building blocks work for other jobs. Library updates: a weekly schedule, one upgrade per PR, changelog read, tests green. SDLC observability: an alert calls a routine's API trigger, Claude investigates and opens a draft fix PR. Migrations at scale: write the playbook as a skill, write evals first, then run many cloud sessions, one per module. These are ideas for after the workshop, not finished tools.

Key points
• Same skills, evals, hooks, schedules, routines
• Different job each time
• Ideas to take home

pass-k-vs-pass-k:
Two ways to read the same runs. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k tries works. pass^k is the chance that all k tries work. With a 75% success rate per try, pass@3 is about 98%, but pass^3 is only about 42% (this exact example is in Anthropic's post). Pick the one that matches the job: if a human picks the best of several tries, pass@k is fine. If the agent runs alone every night, you need pass^k.

Key points
• pass@k = at least one success: 1 − (1 − p)^k
• pass^k = every run succeeds: p^k
• 75% per run → pass@3 ≈ 98%, pass^3 ≈ 42%
• Unattended agents (routines) need pass^k

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
pitfalls:
Four common mistakes from Anthropic's post. Ambiguous task: if two experts would not agree on pass or fail, the task is unclear. Rigid grader: CORE-Bench marked '96.12' wrong because it expected '96.124991…'. Opus 4.5 went from 42% to 95% after fixing grading bugs, unclear task specs and a less constrained setup. Shared state: leftover files or cache from earlier runs can make results look better or fail together; the post mentions Claude reading git history from previous trials. Unread transcripts: always read them, they show why something failed.

Key points
• Two experts should agree on the verdict
• Too-strict graders give fake failures
• Start every trial from a clean environment
• Read the transcripts

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
plan-locally-run-in-the-cloud:
A practical workflow. Plan on your machine in plan mode ('claude --permission-mode plan'), where Claude cannot edit files until you approve the plan. Commit the plan as a file. Start a cloud session that executes it. When it's done, 'claude --teleport' brings the session into your terminal. Teleport is one way: work you do locally after that does not go back to the cloud session.

Key points
• Plan mode blocks edits until you approve
• Commit the plan so the cloud session can read it
• --teleport pulls the session back to your terminal
• Talk locally, wait in the cloud

read-the-delta:
The difference column is the important one. It shows what the plugin adds compared with plain Claude. If a case passes just as well without the plugin (one-off-nit, 0.00), the plugin is not the reason it passes. Either drop the case or make it harder. Big positive numbers show where the skill really helps.

Key points
• Δ = with plugin minus without
• 0.00 means the plugin adds nothing on that case
• Example data, not real results

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals
run-it:
Two commands. 'claude plugin eval init' asks about your plugin, drafts cases and graders, tries them once and writes the files. 'claude plugin eval .' runs the suite. Each case runs 3 times by default, with the plugin and without it, so you get a WITH score, a W/OUT score and the difference. Results go to evals/results/<timestamp>/ with a report.html. In CI, --threshold makes the command fail if a case scores below the limit (default 1.0). The numbers in the table are example data.

Key points
• init drafts the suite for you
• 3 runs per case by default
• Runs with and without the plugin and shows the difference
• --threshold fails CI below a score
• --allow-tools Write because this case writes a file

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals
six-grader-types:
The six grader types in claude plugin eval. Four are free because they only read the transcript and files: regex (a pattern in the reply or a file), tool_used (a tool was called, with min/max counts), tool_order (tool A called before tool B), file_exists (a file was created). Two call a judge model and add cost: llm (passes on a rubric in at least 2 of 3 votes) and baseline (at least as good as a saved reference transcript).

Key points
• Free: regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists
• Cost a model call: llm, baseline
• llm needs 2 of 3 votes to pass
• Good habit: one grader on the result, one on the path

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals
start-from-real-failures:
Don't invent test cases from scratch. Take them from things that actually went wrong: the bug tracker, support tickets, the manual checks you already do, and agent transcripts where it failed. Anthropic's post says 20 to 50 simple tasks from real failures is a great start. You don't need hundreds.

Key points
• Use real failures, not made-up cases
• Sources: bug tracker, support queue, manual checks, transcripts
• 20–50 tasks is enough to start

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
test-both-directions:
A skill only helps if it loads at the right time. Claude decides that from the skill's description, so test the description too. Write prompts that should trigger the skill and near misses that should not, like 'review this PR', which sounds close but is a different job. The Agent Skills guide suggests about 20 queries, a 60/40 split between train and held-out sets, 3 runs per query, and picking the description with the best held-out score. The skill-creator plugin automates this kind of loop.

Key points
• Test when the skill should load and when it shouldn't
• Near misses are the most useful negatives
• ~20 queries, 60/40 split, 3 runs each (Agent Skills guide)
• Choose the description by held-out score, not train score

Sources
https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/optimizing-descriptions

the-environment-is-the-contract:
The environment decides what a cloud session is allowed to do. Network access has four levels: None, Trusted, Custom and Full. Trusted allows a default list: package registries like npm and PyPI, GitHub and cloud SDKs. Custom lets you add your own domains. The setup script runs the first time; if it finishes within about five minutes, the result is saved and reused, and it is rebuilt when the script or allowed hosts change or after about seven days. Environment variables are set per environment. In the demo, only the domains the task needs are green.

Key points
• None / Trusted / Custom / Full
• Trusted = package registries, GitHub, cloud SDKs
• Setup is cached if it finishes in about 5 minutes
• Open only what the task needs

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments
the-eval-loop:
How it works day to day. Write cases, run them 3 times with and without the skill, read the transcripts, fix either the skill or the grader, then run the suite in CI. Repeat on every change to the skill and every time a new model comes out. The plugin eval docs list both: catching regressions when you change the plugin or when a new model is released.

Key points
• Write → run ×3 → read → fix → CI
• Rerun on every skill change
• Rerun on every new model

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals
three-kinds-of-graders:
Three ways to grade, all from Anthropic's post. Code graders (tests, regex, tool-call checks) are fast, cheap and give the same answer every time, but break when a valid answer looks slightly different. Model graders (an LLM with a rubric) handle open-ended output but are not deterministic and need checking against human judgement. Human review is the gold standard but slow and expensive. Anthropic's advice: use deterministic graders where you can.

Key points
• Code: fast, cheap, repeatable, can be too strict
• Model: flexible, needs calibration with humans
• Human: best quality, slow and expensive
• Default to code graders, add others only when needed

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
trust-before-autonomy:
The loop behind the whole talk. Evals give you confidence. Confidence lets you hand more work to cloud agents. Their transcripts show new failures, and those become new eval cases. Each time around, the agent earns a bit more freedom. Anthropic's post makes the same point: read transcripts and turn real failures into tasks.

Key points
• Evals → confidence → cloud agents → transcripts → new cases
• Freedom grows step by step

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
two-themes:
The whole talk is two ideas. First, evals tell you if an agent works, with numbers instead of gut feeling. Second, cloud agents let the agent keep working when you are not at your laptop. The arrow at the bottom is the link: you only give an agent more freedom once evals show you can trust it.

Key points
• Evals = know when it works
• Cloud agents = let it work while you don't
• Trust comes first, then more freedom for the agent
vibes-don-t-scale:
Same prompt, three runs, and one of them goes wrong. Agents are not deterministic: the same input can give a different result each time. If you try it once and it looks fine, you have not proven anything. That is why evals run the same task several times.

Key points
• One good run proves nothing
• Same prompt can give different results
• Run each task several times and count passes
• The example prompt is our workshop skill: cataloguing review comments

Anthropic's post: run multiple trials because outputs vary between runs.

what-runs-the-plant:
What each extra on the plant stands for. Standards board = rules in CLAUDE.md, loaded at the start of every session. Recipe binders = skills; only their descriptions load up front and the full skill loads when needed. Scale and gauge = hooks, commands that run automatically at fixed points like before or after a tool call. Test track = evals. Night shift = a scheduled task on your own machine (desktop scheduled tasks can run as often as every minute). Control centre = a routine in the cloud, started by a schedule, an API call or a GitHub event.

Key points
• CLAUDE.md is loaded every session
• Skills load on demand
• Hooks run every time at set points, not when the model decides
• Scheduled task = your machine; routine = cloud, minimum hourly

when-hillclimbing-pays-off:
Hillclimbing means: change one thing, run the eval again, and keep the change if the score goes up. It only makes sense when three things are true.

Room to improve: if the score is already around 95% or higher, more changes won't add much. Work on cost or speed instead. Bigger than the noise: agents give different results from run to run. If that difference is bigger than the improvement you want, you can't tell a real gain from luck. Run more trials, or stop. One cheap change, one clear result: it works best when a change is quick to make and you can see that the score moved because of that change.

Skills fit this well. Whether a skill loads depends on its description, so the trigger rate depends directly on the one thing you are changing. This is the loop from the 'Test both directions' slide: try a few versions of the description and score them on held-out queries.

Key points
• Hillclimbing = change, run again, keep what raises the score
• Score already ~95% or more: work on cost or speed instead
• The gain must be bigger than the difference between runs
• One cheap change, one score that moves because of it
• Skill descriptions fit this well

Sources
https://claude.dev/blog/automating-eval-design-and-hillclimbing/

when-not-to-use-evals:
Evals are not always worth it. An eval takes work up front and pays you back later, each time you change the skill or a new model comes out. If you only run a skill a few times, that payback may never come. Early on, using the skill yourself and checking the results by hand gets you a long way; Anthropic's post says the same.

Four cases where a full eval suite is not worth it yet. Few uses, early days: the work never pays back. No clear idea of a good result: you are not ready for a suite yet. Still write a few cases by hand, because that makes you decide what a good result is. Only the easy cases: sometimes tasks are picked because they are easy to make or easy to grade, not because they matter. Then the score measures the wrong thing. Too subjective to check: if nobody can check that the grader is right, use human review instead.

The main point: an eval is one signal. If it does not match how the skill is really used, it can make you think things work when they don't. Use it together with production monitoring, user feedback and reading real conversations.

Key points
• Work first, payback later
• Few uses or early days: checking by hand is enough
• No clear idea of a good result yet: write a few cases by hand
• Pick cases that matter, not cases that are easy to grade
• Too subjective: use human review
• Evals are one signal among several

Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

when-something-changes:
Why evals matter when something changes. A new model (the new robot arm) or a changed spec makes the line faster, but the output changes too: the tread pattern is now different. Code review still lets it through because each single diff looks fine. The evals compare the result with the expected outcome and hold the release. After the skill is updated and the evals pass again, you keep the faster model without the wrong output. The plugin eval docs name this use: catching regressions when a new model is released.

Key points
• A new model or spec can change the output quietly
• Review checks one diff, evals check the behaviour
• Evals hold the release until results match
• Fix the skill, keep the upgrade

Sources
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals
where-agents-run:
Four places Claude Code can run. Local session: on your machine with your files. Remote Control: still runs on your machine, but you control it from your phone or browser ('claude remote-control' starts server mode, 'claude --remote-control' an interactive session). Self-hosted environments: cloud sessions on infrastructure your organisation runs; public beta on Team and Enterprise, off by default. Cloud session: an Anthropic-managed VM that keeps going after you close the laptop, started with 'claude --cloud' ('--remote' still works as an old alias).

Key points
• Left side runs on your hardware, right side in managed cloud
• Remote Control: code never leaves your machine
• Self-hosted environments: public beta, Team and Enterprise
• claude --cloud starts a cloud session
